title: The Khalsa's prayer
hook: the whole Khalsa asks to remember the Name, and through it all joy

segments.voice: Yesterday: Takht, and your line: five seats. Which one did you find on the map? For two weeks the Ardas has been remembering. Today, at last, it starts to ask. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

If you were handed one wish for everyone you know, all of them at once, what would you ask for? Most people reach for the big three: health, money, safety. Maybe peace. Those are good wishes. The Ardas has spent its whole first half remembering: the Power, the ten Gurus, the scripture, the five, the four, the forty, the sharers, the martyrs, the Takhts. And now, finally, it turns to its first request. It's a request on behalf of the entire community, everywhere in the world. And what it asks for first isn't health, or money, or safety. Today: the Khalsa's prayer.
screen: `ONE WISH, FOR EVERYONE.` → `HEALTH, MONEY, SAFETY?` → `THE ARDAS'S FIRST REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The request begins: prathme sarbatt khaalsaa jee kee ardaas hai jee. First, this is the prayer of the whole Khalsa. Prathme, first, echoes the very first word of the opening stanza, pritham: first, remember the Power. Sarbatt means all, entire, every one. So before anyone asks for themselves, the prayer is said on behalf of the whole community. And what does the whole Khalsa ask? In paraphrase: may Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru come into the mind. Chit aave. Chit is the mind, the heart's attention. Aave: may it come. The first request is to remember God. Then: chit aavan kaa sadkaa, sarab sukh hove. Sadkaa is a lovely word: by virtue of, as the fruit of, because of. Sarab sukh: all comfort, all happiness. So: by the grace of that remembering, may there be every joy. Look at the order. The joy isn't asked for directly. It's asked for as the fruit of remembering. Sikhs would say that's the whole teaching of the Gurus folded into one sentence. Health, money and safety come and go, as Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks reminded us for a month. The Name is what remains. Ask for that first, and the rest follows from it, or at least can be borne. Notice, too, that the word is repeated: Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru. Three times, slowly, in many gurdwaras. It's the sound of a community trying, together, to make the remembering happen while it asks for it.
screen: `PRATHME: FIRST, FOR THE WHOLE KHALSA.` · `CHIT AAVE: MAY GOD COME TO MIND.` · `SADKAA: AS THE FRUIT OF THAT.` · `SARAB SUKH: EVERY JOY.` · then, large: `THE NAME BRINGS JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the Name once. Sit and let your breath settle. Then, slowly, say Waheguru three times, the way the Ardas does: Waheguru. Waheguru. Waheguru. Leave space between each. Then simply sit, and notice whatever comes after: calm, restlessness, nothing much. That's fine. If you don't pray, you can sit with a word that matters to you instead, and notice what it brings. The bell holds the time.
The Khalsa's prayer. First, for the whole community: may Waheguru come to mind, and by that remembering, every joy.
Your line: the name brings joy. Once today, before you ask for anything, remember first: one breath, one word. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: The petition part of the Ardas begins with a prayer for the whole Khalsa: that Waheguru come to mind, and through that remembrance every comfort; the word Waheguru is said three times.

fork.setup: the Ardas has finished remembering and turns to ask. you're asking for the whole community. what comes first?
options: that Waheguru come to mind, and through it every joy.
fork.reveal: chit aave: may God come to mind. sarab sukh, every joy, is asked as the fruit of that, not on its own.

original.note: Gurmukhi: chit, the mind or the heart's attention; chit aave, may it come to mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Khalsa's prayer asks God for blessings.
what it means: it asks first to remember God, and then for joy as the fruit of remembering.
what a scholar hears: prathme echoes pritham in the opening stanza; sadkaa marks cause, so sarab sukh is grammatically the fruit of chit aavan.
